case_title: Elavarasan v. State rep. by Inspector of Police
accused_occupation: Government servant posted as a Watchman at a PWD bungalow
accused_socioeconomic_status: Government servant; wife stated he earned a monthly salary of Rs.4000 which he handed over for household expenses
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (father of the deceased child; husband of injured wife PW2). Prior dispute over family property with the accused's paternal uncle, not with the victims
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (charged; replaced by s.304 Part II); IPC s.307 (2 counts charged; one count upheld); IPC s.342
weapon: Sharp-edged cutting weapon (Aruval) used on wife and mother; child's fatal injuries possibly caused by a blunt weapon or a hard blow of the bare hand (court's view)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (injured wife PW2) with corroboration from PW1 and PW8; medical (post-mortem and injury reports of PW15, PW16, PW19); observation mahazar Ex.P3; arrest inside house with weapon
aggravating_circumstances: Killing of a child about 1.5 years old; sharp-edged weapon used on wife (who was pregnant) and mother; accused barred the doors and threatened anyone entering
mitigating_circumstances: Sudden quarrel, heat of passion, no premeditation; child was in another room and not connected to the initial fight; sharp weapon not used on child; no cruel or unusual manner
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 (life imprisonment for murder of child); s.342 (1 year RI); s.307 two counts (10 years RI each); sentences concurrent; plea of insanity rejected
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld under s.302, s.307 (one count, attempt on PW2) and s.342; s.307 conviction for attempt on PW3 set aside
offence_finally_established: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder (IPC s.304 Part II) for death of child 'A'; attempt to murder PW2 (IPC s.307, reduced sentence); wrongful confinement (IPC s.342)
neutral_facts: On the night of 11-12 December 2000, the family had gone to bed after dinner around 9 pm. A quarrel broke out between the accused and his wife around midnight, which escalated into an assault around 1 am. The quarrel reportedly arose from the accused's frustration over the sale of family property and his accusations against his wife. During the assault the accused used a sharp-edged cutting weapon on his wife, who was pregnant, causing numerous incised wounds. The accused's mother intervened to save the wife and was also cut with the weapon. The noise and cries woke the couple's young daughter, who was sleeping in an adjacent room and began to cry. The accused went into that room and struck the child, who sustained two injuries, including a fracture, and died. The wife testified as an injured eyewitness to the sequence of events and stated that she did not see the accused strike the child. A post-mortem found the cause of death to be coma resulting from head injuries sustained 24 to 36 hours earlier, consistent with the blunt side of a weapon. Medical reports recorded fifteen injuries on the wife, who was hospitalised for about one and a half months, and six injuries on the mother, two of whose fingers were later amputated. After the incident the accused bolted the doors from inside, refused to open them to police, and threatened to kill anyone who entered. Police, assisted by villagers, forced the door open and found the accused inside the house armed with an Aruval, with the injured women and the child in the house. An observation mahazar recorded writings on the inner walls of the house. Prosecution witnesses, including the mother, gave evidence about the accused's treatment for mental health concerns.
physical_harm: Child 'A' died from head injuries (coma) after two injuries with a fracture; wife suffered 15 injuries and was hospitalised about 1.5 months; mother suffered 6 injuries and loss of two fingers
number_of_offences: 3 sections charged (ss.302, 307 with 2 counts, 342); 3 convictions finally upheld (s.304 Part II replacing s.302, s.307 for PW2, s.342)
premeditation_planning: No premeditation found; the quarrel was sudden and the killing occurred in a sudden fight in the heat of passion
motive: alleged: quarrel over the accused's inability to sell property owned by his mother; the court accepted that the quarrel was sudden
key_evidence_accepted: Deposition of injured wife PW2; corroboration by PW1 and PW8; post-mortem evidence of PW19; injury reports of PW15 and PW16 (Ex.P19, Ex.P20)
witness_credibility: PW2 found completely reliable and unchallenged; PW3 (mother) turned hostile and her evidence about mental disorder was vague and not accepted at face value
post_offence_conduct: Bolted doors from inside, refused to open to police, threatened to kill anyone entering, and was found inside armed with an Aruval; court held that not fleeing did not show insanity
trial_duration: offence: 11-12 December 2000; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 22.3.2006; Supreme Court: 5 July 2011
legal_representation: Appellant: K.K. Mani, Abhishek Krishna, Mayur R. Shah. State/respondent: R. Venkataramani, V.G. Pragasam, Aljo K. Joseph, S. Aristotle, Prabu Ramasubramanian
investigation_status: Charge-sheet filed; committed to sessions; trial completed with 21 prosecution witnesses and court-ordered medical examination
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted (life for s.302; 10 years s.307 x2; 1 year s.342). High Court: appeal dismissed, s.307 conviction for PW3 set aside, others upheld. Supreme Court: partly allowed; s.302 altered to s.304 Part II with 10 years RI; s.307 reduced to 7 years; s.342 upheld
prosecution_argument: Trial and High Court correctly held insanity not proved; no credible evidence of legal insanity at time of offence; not fleeing or attacking without reason does not show unsoundness of mind; relied on Dr. Chandrashekaran's evidence
defence_argument: Material sufficiently proved unsoundness of mind: psychiatric evidence of Dr. Srinivasan, treatment by a psychiatrist, observation mahazar writings, unprovoked assault on family, and post-event conduct
legal_principle_applied: Insanity defence under IPC s.84 must be proved by the accused under Evidence Act s.105 on a preponderance of probabilities, not beyond reasonable doubt; insanity assessed at the time of the offence; intention inferred from weapon and injuries; sudden fight and heat of passion
precedent_relied_upon: Dahyabhai Chhaganbhai Thakkar v. State of Gujarat (1964) 7 SCR 361; State of U.P. v. Ram Swarup and Anr. (1974) 4 SCC 764; Bhikari v. State of Uttar Pradesh AIR 1966 SC 1
sentencing_rationale: No intention to cause death, though knowledge that the injuries were likely to cause death; culpable homicide committed without premeditation in a sudden fight and heat of passion; conviction altered to s.304 Part II with 10 years RI
judicial_mitigating_factors: No premeditation; sudden quarrel in heat of passion; sharp weapon not used on child; did not act in a cruel or unusual manner or take undue advantage
other_sentence_order: Benefit of s.428 CrPC granted; sentences under s.307 and s.342 run concurrently with s.304 Part II sentence; default-of-fine sentence affirmed
